June 15, 2026 
 
Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services 
Department of Health and Human Services 
Attention: RIN 0938-AV44  
 
Submitted via regulations.gov   
  
RE: Medicare and Medicaid Programs; Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act; Interoperability 
Standards and Prior Authorization for Drugs for Medicare Advantage Organizations, Medicaid 
Managed Care Plans, State Medicaid Agencies, Children's Health Insurance Program (CHIP) Agencies 
and CHIP Managed Care Entities, and Issuers of Qualified Health Plans on the Federally-Facilitated 
Exchanges (RIN 0938-AV44) 
On behalf of National Council for Mental Wellbeing (National Council), thank you for the opportunity to 
comment on the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) proposed rule addressing 
interoperability standards and prior authorization for drugs, at 91 Federal Register ("FR") 19890 (April 
14, 2026). National Council is a membership organization representing over 3,200 mental health and 
substance use treatment organizations and the more than 10 million children, adults, and families they 
serve across our nation.  
An essential safeguard in Part D, the 6 protected classes policy ensures that patients managing complex 
health conditions, such as mental illness, are able to access the full spectrum of medications under Part 
D. Specifically, the policy says that Medicare must cover "all or substantially all" medications within the 
six classes (6PC), which includes antidepressants and antipsychotics.   
Under the law, Medicare Part D and MA plans are permitted to manage costs by using utilization management tools like step therapy, and prior authorization within all 6PC classes except HIV. While 
legal, these tools can sometimes lead to unfortunate delays for patients to medication access or 
destabilization of their health condition(s) due to requirements put in place by the health plans.    
The 2026 CMS Interoperability Standards and Prior Authorization for Drugs Proposed Rule addresses 
many of the problems patients face due to utilization management requirements, specifically prior 
authorization. We appreciate the administration's continued focus on improving patient access to health 
care as reflected in the proposed rule, which would create a "more expeditious, transparent and reliable 
process" for prior authorization. While previous efforts have targeted non-drug items and services, we 
are pleased to see CMS address drug access and create pathways for quicker electronic prior 
authorization and increased transparency within the process so that patients and providers can 
understand why and how decisions are made. Many of these proposed changes have the potential to 
reduce administrative burden and improve timely patient access to medically necessary care and 
prescription drugs. 
In particular, CMS proposes that beginning October 1, 2027, state Medicaid and CHIP fee-for-service 
(FFS) programs, Medicaid managed care plans, CHIP managed care entities, and QHP issuers on the FFEs 
must provide a specific reason to providers when denying a prior authorization request for drugs, 
regardless of the method used to send the prior authorization request or decision. National Council 
supports CMS' proposal to provide clear, specific reasons for denials for prior authorization requests for 
drugs. Doing so enables transparent communication that will ultimately help reduce administrative 
burden and help patients receive clear information on their care and can be a part of improving care 
continuity. 
National Council also appreciates CMS' continued efforts to modernize interoperability infrastructure 
and improve electronic prior authorization (ePA) processes. We strongly support the goal of creating 
more standardized, interoperable, and real-time data exchange across payers, providers, and health IT 
systems to improve patient access to timely care. The current prior authorization environment remains 
highly fragmented and administratively burdensome. The proposals to standardize Application 
Programming Interface (API) functionality and data exchange requirements could significantly reduce 
duplicative documentation requests, improve visibility into prior authorization requirements, and 
streamline care coordination for medically complex patients.  
Concurrently, it's vital to recognize that the success of these proposals will depend heavily on vendor 
readiness, operational consistency, and meaningful implementation support for safety-net providers. 
Mental health and substance use providers often lack the financial flexibility or internal IT workforce 
necessary to rapidly adapt to evolving interoperability requirements and frequently rely on a limited 
number of EHR vendors and/or third-party technology partners. The proposed rule appropriately places 
obligations for API readiness and interoperability on impacted payers. However, absent corresponding 
readiness requirements for vendors, we are concerned that providers may face compliance gaps and 
operational disruption despite acting in good faith. CMS should clarify that providers will not be 
penalized for failures attributable to vendors, clearinghouses, or EHR systems outside provider control. 
We further recommend that CMS coordinate implementation timelines closely with the Office of the 
National Coordinator for Health IT (ONC) certification requirements and establish readiness validation or 
testing before enforcement begins. Inconsistent implementation of APIs and varying rollout schedules 
across payers could undermine the efficiencies CMS seeks to create in this proposed rule. 
National Council is also concerned that the expansion of API-based exchange and ePA requirements may 
significantly increase cybersecurity exposure for mental health and substance use providers, which are 
operating with a constrained workforce and infrastructure resources. The proposed rule contemplates a 
broad expansion of interoperable exchanges involving sensitive patient information, yet many provider 
organizations, particularly those serving rural communities, lack dedicated cybersecurity teams or 
advanced IT infrastructure comparable to those of large health systems. Frequently, these IT teams are 
small and usually wear multiple hats, meaning provider organizations rely on third-party vendors and 
organizations to assist them in maintaining HIPAA compliance and securing their data. As 
interoperability requirements expand, CMS must ensure that mental health and substance use provider 
organizations are not absorbing unfunded costs associated with cybersecurity compliance, vendor 
upgrades, API integration, or ongoing maintenance requirements. To ensure provider organizations can 
safely operationalize these changes without compromising patient access or continuity of care, CMS 
should provide technical assistance implementation guidance, cybersecurity and IT workforce 
development support, and dedicated health IT funding opportunities. CMS should also ensure that the 
final implementation framework reflects the operational realities and resource constraints under which 
mental health and substance use providers deliver care.   
Additionally, in response to CMS' request for information on the most significant cybersecurity 
challenges faced by health care provider organizations, National Council highlights that often is the case 
that mental health and substance use providers lack financial resources to procure cybersecurity 
resources beyond what is standard offered by technology vendors they already work with, which can 
make some updated or emerging tools inaccessible. The historic underinvestment in, and patchwork 
system across, mental health and substance use providers, such as being left out of the HITECH Act of 
2009, has significantly contributed to this issue. Additionally, many mental health and substance use 
providers care for people with complex or co-occurring conditions that can also require interaction with 
providers across the broader health care system (from hospitals to emergency rooms and primary care 
settings). Data sharing among these groups is a priority, however, integration can expose mental health 
and substance use organizations to other organizations' security risks. Aside from further, strategic 
investment in cybersecurity for mental health and substance use providers, resources and tools that 
support providers to put recovery plans in place would be beneficial.
analysis:
## 1. COMMENTER INFORMATION

- **Author/Organization name:** National Council for Mental Wellbeing (National Council)
- **Stakeholder type:** Professional Association
- **Credentials or expertise mentioned:** Membership organization representing over 3,200 mental health and substance use treatment organizations serving more than 10 million children, adults, and families; represented by Reyna Taylor, Senior Vice President, Public Policy & Advocacy

---

## 2. EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

The National Council for Mental Wellbeing generally supports the proposed rule's goals of expediting and improving transparency in prior authorization, particularly the PA-DENIAL-REASONS provision. However, the organization raises significant concerns about cybersecurity risks and resource constraints facing mental health and substance use providers—a population historically underinvested in health IT—and urges CMS to provide technical assistance, workforce support, and dedicated funding, and to clarify that providers will not be penalized for vendor failures outside their control.

---

## 3. REGULATORY CONTEXT

- **Specific provisions addressed:** PA-DENIAL-REASONS, PA-DRUG-MEDICAL, PA-DRUG-PHARMACY, FHIR-IG-REQUIRED (general support for API standardization)
- **Regulatory citations mentioned:** 91 FR 19890 (April 14, 2026); RIN 0938-AV44; Medicare Part D 6 protected classes policy; HITECH Act of 2009
- **Standards referenced:** Application Programming Interface (API), electronic prior authorization (ePA), HIPAA

---

## 4. DETAILED POSITIONS

**Topic 1: PA Denial Reasons**
- **Provision ID:** PA-DENIAL-REASONS
- **Position:** Support
- **Rationale:** Clear denial reasons enable transparent communication, reduce administrative burden, and help patients understand their care decisions, supporting care continuity.
- **Specific request:** Support the October 1, 2027 requirement that Medicaid/CHIP FFS, managed care plans, and QHP issuers provide specific reasons for drug PA denials.

**Topic 2: API Standardization and ePA**
- **Provision ID:** PA-DRUG-MEDICAL, PA-DRUG-PHARMACY, FHIR-IG-REQUIRED
- **Position:** Support with modifications
- **Rationale:** Standardized, interoperable, real-time data exchange can reduce duplicative documentation and improve care coordination for medically complex patients. However, mental health and substance use providers depend heavily on a limited number of EHR vendors and third-party technology partners.
- **Specific request:** CMS should clarify that providers will not be penalized for failures attributable to vendors, clearinghouses, or EHR systems outside provider control; coordinate timelines with ONC certification requirements; establish readiness validation or testing before enforcement begins.

**Topic 3: Cybersecurity Risks for Safety-Net Providers**
- **Provision ID:** GENERAL
- **Position:** Concerns
- **Rationale:** The expansion of API-based exchange significantly increases cybersecurity exposure for mental health and substance use providers, which often lack dedicated cybersecurity teams, operate with constrained IT resources, and were historically excluded from HITECH Act funding. Rural providers are particularly vulnerable. Integration with broader health systems also exposes these organizations to third-party security risks.
- **Specific request:** CMS should provide technical assistance guidance, cybersecurity and IT workforce development support, and dedicated health IT funding; ensure the final framework reflects operational realities of mental health and substance use providers; support recovery planning tools.

---

## 5. SOLICITATION RESPONSES

- **S16:** Commenter supports requiring specific denial reasons; emphasizes value for transparent communication, reduced administrative burden, and care continuity for mental health and substance use patients.
- **S37:** Commenter highlights implementation challenges for safety-net providers—specifically mental health and substance use organizations—citing limited IT staff, reliance on third-party vendors, and resource constraints as barriers.
- **S18 (implicit):** Commenter notes that mandatory IG/API requirements place obligations on payers but the corresponding burden on providers and vendor readiness is not addressed; calls for provider protections.

---

## 6. RECOMMENDATIONS

1. Support the PA-DENIAL-REASONS provision requiring specific reasons when denying drug PA requests.
2. Clarify that providers will not be penalized for compliance failures attributable to vendors, clearinghouses, or EHR systems outside their control.
3. Coordinate implementation timelines closely with ONC certification requirements.
4. Establish readiness validation or testing before enforcement begins.
5. Provide technical assistance and implementation guidance to mental health and substance use providers.
6. Provide cybersecurity and IT workforce development support and dedicated health IT funding for safety-net providers.
7. Ensure the final implementation framework reflects operational realities and resource constraints of mental health and substance use providers.
8. Invest strategically in cybersecurity resources for mental health and substance use providers, including recovery plan support tools.

---

## 7. CONCERNS & OBJECTIONS

- **Primary concerns:** Cybersecurity risks and unfunded mandates for mental health and substance use providers; vendor readiness gaps that could cause provider compliance failures through no fault of their own.
- **Potential negative impacts cited:** Compliance gaps and operational disruption for safety-net providers; increased cybersecurity exposure for organizations with limited IT staff; unfunded costs for cybersecurity compliance, vendor upgrades, API integration, and maintenance.
- **Implementation barriers mentioned:** Limited financial flexibility; small IT teams wearing multiple hats; historic underinvestment (exclusion from HITECH Act 2009); reliance on third-party vendors; rural providers lacking advanced IT infrastructure; exposure to other organizations' security risks through data sharing.

---

## 8. SUPPORTING EVIDENCE

- **Data or statistics cited:** National Council represents over 3,200 mental health and substance use treatment organizations serving 10 million+ children, adults, and families.
- **Studies or research referenced:** References to HITECH Act of 2009 and its exclusion of mental health and substance use providers.
- **Examples provided:** Rural community providers lacking dedicated cybersecurity teams; small IT teams maintaining HIPAA compliance with third-party vendor support; data sharing exposures when integrating with hospitals, ERs, and primary care.

---

## 9. IMPACT ASSESSMENT

- **Affected stakeholders:** Mental health and substance use treatment providers (3,200+ organizations); patients with mental illness and substance use disorders (10M+); rural communities; EHR vendors and third-party technology partners.
- **Economic implications:** Unfunded costs for cybersecurity compliance, vendor upgrades, API integration, and maintenance would fall on resource-constrained safety-net providers.
- **Technical feasibility:** Feasible in principle but constrained by limited IT workforce, vendor readiness gaps, and lack of dedicated funding for this provider population.
- **Patient care impact:** Positive if implemented well—faster PA decisions and clearer denial reasons improve access for mental health and substance use patients. Risk of care disruption if implementation failures occur.

---

## 10. SENTIMENT ANALYSIS

- **Overall position:** Mixed (Supportive of goals, Concerned about implementation)
- **Tone:** Professional, Collaborative
- **Priority level:** Medium

---

## 11. KEY QUOTES

1. "CMS should clarify that providers will not be penalized for failures attributable to vendors, clearinghouses, or EHR systems outside provider control." - Context: Raising concern that API obligations fall on payers but implementation gaps may manifest at the provider level.

2. "The historic underinvestment in, and patchwork system across, mental health and substance use providers, such as being left out of the HITECH Act of 2009, has significantly contributed to this issue." - Context: Explaining why mental health and substance use providers face greater cybersecurity challenges than other provider types.

3. "As interoperability requirements expand, CMS must ensure that mental health and substance use provider organizations are not absorbing unfunded costs associated with cybersecurity compliance, vendor upgrades, API integration, or ongoing maintenance requirements." - Context: Urging CMS to accompany expanded requirements with dedicated funding and support.

---

## 12. THEMES

- [x] **IMPLEMENTATION-TIMELINE** - Recommends coordinating timelines with ONC certification and establishing readiness validation before enforcement.
- [x] **COST-RESOURCES** - Highlights unfunded costs of cybersecurity compliance, vendor upgrades, and API integration for underfunded safety-net providers.
- [x] **PROVIDER-BURDEN** - Focus on administrative and operational burden on mental health and substance use providers with constrained resources.
- [x] **PRIVACY-SECURITY** - Detailed concern about cybersecurity risks for providers with limited IT staff and infrastructure, especially given sensitive behavioral health data.
- [x] **HEALTH-EQUITY** - Focus on mental health and substance use providers serving underserved populations, including rural communities; highlights historic underinvestment.
- [x] **PATIENT-ACCESS** - Supports PA improvements to reduce barriers for patients managing complex mental health conditions; notes risk of care destabilization from utilization management.
- [x] **STAKEHOLDER-COORDINATION** - Recommends CMS coordinate with ONC; notes need for vendor readiness requirements alongside payer obligations.
- [x] **TRANSPARENCY** - Supports PA-DENIAL-REASONS provision as key to transparency and care continuity.
- [x] **VENDOR-ECOSYSTEM** - Central concern about reliance on EHR vendors and third-party technology partners; calls for vendor readiness requirements and provider protections.
